newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian pensions under strain as population ages.
newsitem.headline: Italian pensions under strain as population ages.

text.p: Italy's state pensions system is coming under growing strain as the economy languishes and unemployment rises, forcing a shrinking working population to maintain a growing army of elderly people.
And nearly two years after reforms to the deficit-ridden system were hailed as a turning point, employers are warning Prime Minister Romano Prodi of a crisis ahead.

"We are unhappy with the reforms because the country was led to believe that the pensions problem had been solved," said Carlo Callieri, the President of the Italian employers' federation Confindustria in a recent televised debate.

Prodi has said he will a honour a pledge made the in a pensions reform deal in 1995 not to touch present arrangements until next year. Trade unions have threatened mass protests if changes to the system are brought forward.
At the heart of the problem is Italy's extremely low birth rate which threatens over time to shrink the working population at a time when average life expectancy has never been higher.

Italy already has one of the highest "dependency ratios" -- a measure of the elderly as a proportion of the working population -- in the western world and demographers expect it to rise relentlessly in the years ahead.
"We have 18 million pensions which are being paid for by 21 million working people," said Callieri.
Critics argue that the state pensions system, even after the 1995 reforms, is simply beyond Italy's means as it pays out pensions worth up to 80 percent of final salary.

On present trends, Italy's pensions bill is set to climb from 242 trillion lire in 1995 to 318 trillion in 2010 before sky-rocketing to 500.5 trillion lire by 2030, according to figures compiled by Milan business daily Il Sole 24 Ore.
Meanwhile, Italy's population between the ages of 15 and 70 is seen falling gently from 42.86 million in 1995 to 41.26 million in 2010 before plunging to 36.68 million in 2030, Il Sole 24 Ore said.

Like many European countries, Italy operates a so-called "pay-as-you-go" pensions system under which handouts to the retired are paid from contributions drawn from those in work and from their employers.
The system flourished in the 1960s when the economy boomed and Italy enjoyed something approaching full employment for the first time in its recent history.
With a high birth rate and a growing labour force the state pensions institute, INPS, was able to guarantee pensions for practically everybody and to balance its books.

Today INPS is running an annual deficit of around 80 trillion lire ($50.31 billion) which has to be plugged with massive injections of cash from the Treasury. The deficit is bloated by the institute's obligation to grant basic pensions to poor people who have paid no contributions into the system.

Many believe the Dini reforms, which came into force at the beginning of 1996, are too slow to take effect, place too heavy a burden on those in work and on their employers and will not cut deep enough into a widening INPS deficit in the years ahead.
"The Dini law is not enough," said Giulio Tremonti, a former Budget minister in the centre-right administration led by media magnate-turned-politician Silvio Berlusconi in 1994.
"This system takes away from those who work without guaranteeing a future for those who do not work," Tremonti said.
The main innovation of the Dini reform was to change the way the value of benefits are calculated when people retire and start to draw a pension.
The new system, which will not become fully effective until 2030, will base old age pensions on the value of contributions paid into the system over an individual's entire working life.
Until now pension payouts reflect salary levels in the final years of employment.

This means that a generation of young Italians is growing up which cannot rely on the pension arrangements granted to their parents. The government recently passed legislation allowing companies to set up funds for top-up pensions.
"There is going to be a big push towards top-up pensions. For young people it is going to be a necessity," said Sergio Corbello, President of Assoprevidenza, the pension funds association.

The reform also decreed that all those who had been paying into a state pension scheme for at least 18 years will be entitled to an old-style pension while those with less than 18 years will qualify for new, less generous, contributions-based payouts when they retire.

"One can debate whether the transition to the new system is too long but the reform yields 100 trillion lire in savings over 10 years," said Beniamino La Padula, an economist at the CGIL trade union confederation in Rome.

Critics say the Dini reforms do not go far or fast enough in stamping out one of the anomalies of Italy's welfare state -- an entitlement to early retirement on full pension after 35 years of paying contributions into the system.

Pension conditions under the state umbrella also vary widely from one industry to the next -- with agricultural workers paying far lower contributions into the system than industrial employees but drawing similar-sized payouts when they retire.

The reform will raise the threshold for early retirement to 40 years service but it will still be possible in future for people to stop working at 57 and draw so-called "seniority pensions", below the new statutory retirement age of 65 for men and 60.
"The biggest drawback (of the reform) are the seniority pensions. Even in 2020 people will be drawing pensions from their mid-fifties," said Callieri.
"At 55 you can expect to live until you are 80 but if you retire at 65 you will draw a pension for a much shorter period," Callieri added.
The government is now turning its attention to the patchwork of special privileges for certain categories of workers, notably airline pilots and central bank employees.
Bank of Italy employees can retire on a pension at 50 and airline pilots at 45. The government wants to gradually raise these thresholds but is expected to encounter stiff resistance.
Favoured treatment received by farm workers is a legacy of the Cold War era when governments assiduously courted the agricultural vote, seen as a bastion of anti-communism.
The result is that INPS currently pays out annually more than 10 trillion lire in pensions to retired farm workers but only receives 1.9 trillion lire in contributions from those still in work.
But even the harshest critics of the new-look pensions system concede it does introduce a significant self-righting mechanism which could help ward off a full-blown crisis if things get out of hand.

The value of a pension in the reformed system is calculated by totting up contributions paid over an entire working life and adjusting them using a special formula, known as a "conversion coefficient". The new pensions law allows the government to review the coefficient every 10 years to take account of demographic trends.
"The fact that the coefficient can be varied means that there is a possibility of reforming the pensions system from within," said Assoprevidenza's Corbello.
